title: What Students Lose When They Know They’re Right
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer turns from his usual concern with wrong answers to the opportunity cost of telling students they are right. Using a Desmos card sort taught to seventh graders, he explains why the platform knows whether a sort is correct but deliberately withholds that verdict from students. He describes three things that survive that choice: self-reflection when students test ideas in an earlier task, richer group discussion when groups reconcile differences with no pre-settled answer, and whole-class discussion built on the card most often misplaced. His broader claim is that computers are good at only certain kinds of feedback, usually evaluative, and that immediate right-or-wrong feedback can cost students chances to learn about mathematics and themselves as mathematicians. He backs this with ISTE standards that favor timely rather than immediate feedback. The post ends with a short run of unrelated news items.
points: Withholding correctness is a design choice: the platform knows the answer but keeps students thinking rather than checking.
Without a green check mark, students return to earlier work and transfer understanding between tasks instead of guess-and-check.
Group comparison of card sorts stays mathematically rich only when debates are not pre-settled by the computer.
Aggregated class data on the most-missed card makes a strong whole-class conversation starter.
Computer feedback is typically evaluative and limited to certain kinds of thinking, and sometimes a human gives the best feedback.

But computers are only good at providing certain kinds of feedback and only on certain kinds of thinking. And that feedback is often evaluative–immediately telling students they are right or wrong.
